title: Division without undefined behavior

tests.expr: ({ volatile int32_t a = INT32_MIN, b = -1; c_div(a, b); })
({ volatile int32_t a = INT32_MIN, b = -1; c_mod(a, b); })
({ volatile int32_t a = INT32_MAX, b = -1; c_div(a, b); })

hints: C's `/` and `%` already truncate toward zero and give the remainder the dividend's sign, exactly like .uir. Only one input pair is a problem.
The problem is `INT_MIN / -1`: the true answer, 2^31, doesn't fit in `int32_t`, so C calls it undefined (on x86 it traps). Same for `INT_MIN % -1`. Handle `b == -1` before dividing.
When `b == -1`, the quotient is `-a` with wraparound and the remainder is always 0. Negate through `uint32_t` (`0u - (uint32_t)a`) so even `-INT_MIN` wraps instead of overflowing.
explain: Dividing by -1 is the only way `/` or `%` can overflow, so the solution answers it without dividing: `0u - (uint32_t)a` negates with wraparound (giving INT_MIN for INT_MIN), and any number mod -1 is 0. Every other pair goes to C's own `/` and `%`, which already match .uir's truncating semantics. The INT_MIN tests use `volatile` operands so the compiler can't fold the division away at compile time, and the runner traps undefined behavior, so a plain `a / b` fails them.
